structure.title: From ordinary morality
structure.text: The first section develops the idea of a good will from familiar judgments about duty and motivation.

structure.title: Principle and freedom
structure.text: The second seeks morality's supreme principle; the third examines why rational agents should understand themselves as bound by it.

people.name: Good will
people.text: For Kant, the only thing good without qualification: a will that acts from duty, whatever the results turn out to be.

people.name: Maxim
people.text: The personal rule behind an action, such as 'I will make a false promise when I need money'; Kant asks whether it could be a law for everyone.

people.name: Autonomy
people.text: The idea that a rational being gives itself the moral law rather than taking it from outside, which for Kant is the source of human dignity.

context.title: Duty and inclination
context.text: An action can match duty while being motivated by advantage. Kant asks what gives an action moral worth.
context.takeaway: Separate outward conformity from the reason for acting.

context.title: Universal law
context.text: The proposed test concerns the principle of one's action, not whether everyone could reproduce its exact circumstances.
context.takeaway: State the maxim before testing it.

notice.text: Follow the same examples through different formulations.
notice.why: They reveal how the proposed principles relate.

notice.text: Notice the distinction between price and dignity.
notice.why: It changes what may be exchanged for a desired result.

opening: You need money and know nobody will lend it unless you promise to repay. You also know you cannot keep the promise. Kant takes this ordinary temptation seriously enough to ask what a promise would become if everyone treated it that way. His search for morality's foundation strips away reputation, convenience, and the hope of reward. It leads to a demanding account of freedom in which another person's humanity places limits on what you may do, even for a result you badly want.
